newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Corn Exchange finally loses trading floor.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Corn Exchange finally loses trading floor.

text.p: London's centuries-old Corn Exchange, the historic centre of Britain's grain trade, has finally lost the floor it uses for business due to the changing structure of the grain market.

In a letter sent to members of the Baltic Exchange, a hub of the world shipping trade, secretary Simon Clark said an agreement to end the Corn Exchange's right to use the Baltic trading floor had been finalised.

The Corn Exchange had used the floor since 1987 but attendance had dwindled over the years. It received a 150,000 pounds sterling payment as compensation for the agreement's termination, Clark told Reuters.
Baltic Exchange members each received an interim dividend of 1,500 pounds.

The Baltic will continue to operate a bourse twice a year to give grain traders a chance to meet informally. The next Corn Bourse will be held on May 9, followed by another on November 28, the letter said.
Grain trading, as conducted by the Corn Exchange, dwindled as traded quantities became larger and more transactions became based on government business.
Many brokers and merchants also opted to move out of London to cut overheads, finding that improved communications reduced the need for a formal marketplace.
